description: NASA is preparing humanity's return to the Moon, but choosing where and when to land is a complex challenge. By combining lunar terrain data with sunlight and Earth-visibility analysis, our platform transforms raw space data into intelligent mission decisions.
summary: Project OPUS is LunaWise, a web tool that answers one question for commercial lunar landers: the launch slipped, so which south pole sites still work? At the lunar south pole the Sun and Earth sit only a few degrees above the horizon, so a ridge can decide whether a lander gets power and radio contact. LunaWise computes, hour by hour for 2027, whether the Sun and Earth clear the real terrain at five candidate sites: Connecting ridge, Shackleton rim, the peak near Shackleton, de Gerlache rim and Malapert massif. A planner sets a landing date, a launch slip, a mission length and their own requirements. The tool shows which sites meet them, which fail, and the first hour and direction of the failure. A 3D digital twin lets users walk the terrain and watch the Sun and Earth move. Every number comes from NASA data and our own computation, with no invented scores. This helps planners compare sites and dates quickly and see why a site fails.
details:
Sun and Earth positions: computed with NASA SPICE (NAIF) in the Moon’s mean-Earth frame for every hour of 2027, and cross-checked against JPL Horizons.

Terrain: LRO LOLA elevation data (5 m site maps and the 20 m south pole grid from NASA PGDA) is turned into a horizon skyline for each site at 0, 2, 5 and 10 m mast heights.

The core test: for each hour, is the Sun or Earth higher than the terrain horizon in its direction? That gives lit and visible flags, and from them sunlight %, Earth visibility %, longest night and longest communication blackout.

Mission logic: a landing date, a launch slip and requirements are applied to those flags to find the first failure and explain it in plain language.

Static delivery: results are precomputed into static JSON, so the app runs without a backend.

Benefits and intended impact

A planner can see in seconds how a delay changes each site, and which direction of terrain blocks Earth.

It shows that no single site wins on everything, so choice depends on the mission.

Anyone can open it from a public link to explore the same data.

Tools and technologies

Python (spiceypy, numpy, rasterio, pyproj) for the pipeline.

JavaScript and Three.js for the web app and 3D twin, hosted on Cloudflare Workers.

NASA data and tools: SPICE, JPL Horizons, LRO/LOLA (PGDA, Barker et al. 2021), PGDA product 69 Goddard maps, Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap.

Automated tests in pytest and Node for the pipeline, horizon masks and mission logic.

Creativity

We start from the planner’s real problem, a launch delay, not from a map.

One simple test (body above terrain horizon) drives every view: skyline chart, timeline, comparison and 3D twin.

The 3D view is a visual aid, with a ray-cast consistency check against the engine.

Validity and honesty

We compared our results with NASA Goddard’s long-term illumination and Earth-visibility maps and show the differences openly. The 0 m and 2 m mast results bracket Goddard’s sunlight values, and the gaps are consistent with pixel size, time span and observer height.

Limits: about 90% of the 5 m terrain pixels are interpolated between laser spots; the data covers 2027 only; the battery model is a scenario assumption, not NASA data; custom clicked points use approximate estimates and are not validated.

Synthetic data exists only as a labelled fallback when files are missing, and no result for the five sites uses it.

Factors we considered

Low Sun and Earth angles at the pole, observer height, terrain uncertainty, coordinate frame consistency, and keeping the demo reliable offline.
